why: Direct firm-level measure of corruption friction — when bribe demands on businesses spike, it signals eroding state legitimacy and weakens the economic conditions that precede political crisis. Complements V-Dem corruption indices with a behavioural, survey-grounded signal rather than expert assessment.
coverage_note: Enterprise Survey coverage is irregular — roughly 3-5-year gaps per country; concentrated in lower-middle-income and IDA countries; many high-income and small-island states absent.

trends.reason: Firm-level bribery is the most direct behavioural proxy for the corruption deterioration that precedes and accompanies this Trend's canonical shape.
Rising bribery burdens raise operating costs and deter investment, contributing to the economic slowdown pattern.
High bribery rates co-occur with weak rule of law environments where repression is more likely.
Corruption grievances are a noted protest mobilisation trigger but this indicator is survey-based with long lags, limiting temporal precision.

why: Aggregates constitutional constraints on executive power, rule of law, and individual liberties into a single latent score — captures the institutional erosion trajectory that precedes democratic backsliding, political repression, and mass mobilisation. Its continuous scale makes multi-year movement shapes learnable by XGBoost walks.
coverage_note: V-Dem near-universal coverage; pre-1945 estimates rely on sparse historical coding and carry wider uncertainty intervals.

trends.reason: Declining liberal index is the canonical leading signal of executive power consolidation — directly measures the erosion of checks this Trend captures.
Liberal constraints breakdown directly precedes and enables systematic repression; strong theoretical and empirical alignment.
Rising liberal scores are the definitional signal of democratisation — a top feature candidate for this Trend's run-up shape.
Constitutional rewrites often coincide with liberal index inflections; contributes movement shape information.
Liberal erosion is a documented protest trigger; movement shape plausibly aligns with protest escalation window.

why: Remittance inflows as a share of GDP reveal diaspora-dependency — high ratios signal fragile domestic labour markets and exposure to external income shocks, while sudden remittance collapses historically precede currency and fiscal stress in remittance-dependent states.
coverage_note: WB WDI series; good coverage from 1995 onward; early 1990s sparse for post-Soviet and small-island states; informal flows systematically undercounted in high-remittance countries.

trends.reason: Remittance collapse is a documented trigger of balance-of-payments stress; high dependency amplifies exchange-rate vulnerability preceding currency crises.
Remittance-dependent economies are especially exposed to global slowdowns; sudden drops translate directly into consumption and fiscal contractions.
High remittance ratios proxy large diaspora stocks, themselves a signal of prior or ongoing displacement pressure from origin countries.
Remittance dependency concentrates income gains in migrant households, structurally shaping inequality dynamics; marginal orthogonal signal.

why: Core Civil Society Index measures the organisational health and autonomy of civil society — its decline is a leading indicator of political closure and repression, while high levels predict mobilisation capacity for democratic transitions and mass protests; captures a dimension not fully reflected in electoral or institutional indices.
coverage_note: V-Dem near-universal coverage; pre-WWII estimates rely on thin expert codings; post-1990 series most reliable for ML training.

trends.reason: Civil society suppression is both a mechanism and signal of political repression — declining CCSI traces the canonical run-up shape for this Trend.
Strong civil society is a robust predictor and enabler of successful democratic transitions; rising CCSI is a key leading signal.
Civil society organisational capacity determines protest mobilisation potential; CCSI captures the enabling environment for this Trend.
Executives consolidating power systematically curtail civil society; co-movement provides complementary signal to other V-Dem governance indicators.
Civil society suppression accompanies and enables human rights violations; moderate orthogonal contribution alongside CCSI sub-components.

why: State territorial control is a foundational fragility signal — when governments lose effective control over parts of their territory to warlords or rebels, it directly precedes or accompanies civil conflict escalation, insurgency, and humanitarian crises; captures a state-failure dimension distinct from institutional quality indices.
coverage_note: V-Dem near-universal; pre-1945 codings estimated from historical sources with wider uncertainty; post-1989 most reliable for conflict-focused Trends.

trends.reason: Territorial control loss is both a cause and effect of insurgency — the sharpest available signal for this Trend's onset and escalation shape.
Territorial fragmentation triggers displacement and access denial; strong leading signal for humanitarian deterioration.
Territorial control erosion often precedes military intervention as armies act to restore order; plausible top-40 feature.
External actors intervene when host governments lose territorial control; provides movement shape signal for this Trend.
Ungoverned spaces enable communal group clashes; territorial control is a plausible contributory feature.

why: Aggregate forced displacement (refugees + asylum-seekers + IDPs) provides a composite headline measure of the cumulative human cost of instability — its multi-year trajectory captures both conflict intensity and state failure duration in a single ML-ready feature, with strong predictive signal for humanitarian and conflict Trends.
coverage_note: UNHCR annual data; pre-2000 IDP estimates less systematic; derived composite requires consistent sub-series availability; small-island states may have near-zero values creating structural zeros.

trends.reason: Total forced displacement is the aggregate outcome variable for humanitarian crises — cumulative stock captures crisis duration and intensity together.
Displacement magnitude tracks conflict intensity closely; the composite aggregates multiple UNHCR signals into a single high-signal feature.
Directly measures the phenomenon this Trend captures; most likely to enter greedy top features for this recipe.
State repression generates refugee and asylum flows; composite stock reflects cumulative persecution pressure.
High displacement levels trigger peacekeeping deployments; stock trajectory aligns with pre-agreement escalation shape.

why: Horizontal accountability — the capacity of legislatures, judiciaries, and oversight bodies to constrain the executive — is a leading indicator of institutional degradation and authoritarian drift; its decline traces the gradual erosion of checks that precedes coups, power consolidation, and political repression.
coverage_note: V-Dem near-universal; pre-WWII estimates carry wider uncertainty; most reliable and most relevant for post-1945 democratic contexts.

trends.reason: Declining horizontal accountability is the definitional precursor to executive consolidation — captures the institutional weakening trajectory that precedes this Trend's terminating event.
Weak institutional checks remove constraints on military intervention; horacc decline is an established coup precursor in the literature.
Constitutional rewrites that concentrate power typically track horacc inflections; movement shape alignment plausible.
Weak oversight enables corruption; co-movement provides signal complementary to direct corruption measures.
Accountability institution strengthening is a key marker of genuine democratisation; rising horacc traces transition run-up.

why: Aggregate best-estimate deaths across all organised violence types (state-based, non-state, one-sided) provides the most comprehensive single lethality signal — capturing the full violence environment of a country-year rather than any one conflict type, making it a broad-spectrum conflict intensity feature for QGI recipes.
coverage_note: UCDP GED covers conflict-affected countries only; zero-violence countries absent or coded zero from 1989; pre-1989 not available; data most complete for Africa, Middle East, Asia.

trends.reason: Total deaths aggregate captures civil war intensity trajectory directly; highly likely to be a top greedy feature for this Trend.
Mass casualties are both a cause and core indicator of humanitarian crisis; aggregate deaths provide a strong leading and concurrent signal.
GED includes one-sided violence and non-state conflict deaths from terrorism-adjacent events; aggregate trajectory traces terrorist escalation patterns.
Total organised violence deaths is the broadest direct measure of the phenomenon this Trend captures.
High total lethality thresholds historically trigger foreign intervention; aggregate deaths proxy the severity threshold that prompts external action.

why: Freedom of association — covering rights to form parties, civil society organisations, and trade unions — captures the civic space contraction that precedes and accompanies political repression and executive consolidation; its decline is a more targeted signal than broad civil liberties indices for mobilisation-blocking dynamics.
coverage_note: V-Dem near-universal; pre-1945 coding sparse and expert-estimated; contemporary series (post-1990) most informative for political Trends.

trends.reason: Association rights suppression is a primary mechanism of political repression; directly traces the civic-space closure trajectory that defines this Trend's shape.
Executives consolidating power systematically restrict party competition and civil organisation; declining frassoc co-moves with consolidation trajectory.
Opening of association rights is a leading indicator and enabling condition for democratic transitions; rising scores trace the run-up shape.
Association freedom enables protest organising; restrictions on it shift mobilisation patterns in ways relevant to this Trend's occurrence timing.
Trade union rights are a core sub-component of frassoc; association freedom directly governs labour organising capacity relevant to this Trend.

why: Gender Inequality Index aggregates reproductive health gaps, empowerment deficits, and labour market exclusion into a single structural inequality score — high GII values signal marginalised female participation that correlates with broader governance deficits, social fragility, and susceptibility to poverty and mobilisation crises.
coverage_note: UNDP HDR; coverage good for 160+ countries from 1995; small-island and micro-state gaps; GII computation requires multiple sub-indicators so countries missing any sub-component are excluded from that year.

trends.reason: GII is a composite structural inequality measure; high and worsening GII traces the inequality trajectory that precedes and accompanies poverty crisis events.
High gender inequality predicts worse humanitarian outcomes — women and girls bear disproportionate crisis costs; contributes background fragility signal.
Gender inequality is a primary policy reform target; GII trajectories may align with reform onset and outcome measurement windows.
Gender grievances have mobilised significant protests globally but GII is a slow-moving structural indicator with limited temporal precision for event-level prediction.
Gender empowerment tracks democratic development but GII is a lagging structural measure; marginal orthogonal contribution beyond governance indices.
